TITLE: A Comparison of Lake Trout Spawning, Fry Emergence, and Habitat Use in Lakes Michigan, Huron, and Champlain
SPECIES: T1=Salvelinus namaycush (lake trout, stocked lake trout, Lake trout); T2=Perca flavescens (yellow perch); T3=Coregonus clupeaformis (lake whitefish); T4=Micropterus dolomieu (smallmouth bass); T5=Petromyzon marinus (sea lamprey)
CONTEXT: The purpose of this study was to compare lake trout spawning populations, spawning habitat use, egg deposition, and fry emergence among three lakes representing different stages of lake trout population restoration. In Lake Michigan, the restoration program has been underway since 1965; evidence of reproduction (egg deposition and/or fry hatch) was documented in the Grand Traverse Bay area in the early 1970s, and along the southern shoreline in the early 1980s and 1990s, but year classes of wild age-1+ fish have not been detected. In all three lakes, potential spawning sites were located using data on fall aggregations of lake trout, and lake bottom topography and substrate composition. Information on lake trout aggregations was available in historic records from fall commercial fishing and agency assessment work in lakes Michigan and Huron (Goodyear et al. 1982, [ref]), from modern lake trout assessment work in Lakes Champlain and Huron (D. Reid, OMNR, Owen Sound, ON, pers. comm.), and assessment of egg deposition at reefs in Parry Sound (J. Fitzsimons, unpub. data). Spawning reefs used by lake trout generally have deep cobbles that protect eggs over the winter, and a steep slope that may aid in increasing water currents that keep the substrate scoured of silt (Fitzsimons 1994, [ref]). We examined bathymetric charts for areas of steep contour, then examined promising sites using scuba. If rubble/cobble substrates were present, we measured the following characteristics at each site: depth at top and base of the reef, reef area (defined by the area encompassed by cobbles), slope angle of the reef contour, substrate type, particulate substrate size, interstitial depth, presence of silt or organic debris, and presence of zebra mussels. Additional sites were sampled as time allowed.
TEXT:
[1] (abs) ABSTRACT.
[2] (abs) Restoration of self-sustaining populations of lake trout is underway in all of the Great Lakes and Lake Champlain, but restoration has only been achieved in Lake Superior and in Parry Sound, Lake Huron.
[3] (abs) We evaluated progress toward restoration by comparing spawning habitat availability, spawner abundance, egg and fry density, and egg survival in Parry Sound in Lake Huron, in Lake Michigan, and in Lake Champlain in 2000–2003.
[4] (abs) Divers surveyed and assessed abundance of spawners at 5 to 15 sites in each lake.
[5] (abs) Spawning adults were sampled using standardized gill nets, eggs were sampled using egg bags, and fry were sampled using emergent fry traps and egg bags left on spawning reefs overwinter.
[6] (abs) Spawning habitat was abundant in each lake.
[7] (abs) Adult lake trout abundance was low in Lake Michigan and Parry Sound, and very high at one site in Lake Champlain.
[8] (abs) Egg deposition was lowest in Lake Michigan (0.4–154.5 eggs•m–2, median = 1.7), intermediate in Parry Sound (39–1,027 eggs•m–2, median = 278), and highest in Lake Champlain (0.001–9,623 eggs•m–2, median = 652).
[9] (abs) Fry collections in fry traps followed the same trend: no fry in Lake Michigan, 0.005–0.06 fry•trap–1 day–1 in Parry Sound, and 0.08–3.6 fry•trap–1 in Lake Champlain.
[10] (abs) Egg survival to hatch in overwinter egg bags was similar in Lake Michigan (7.6%) and Parry Sound (2.3–8.9%) in 2001–02, and varied in Lake Champlain (0.4–1.1% in 2001–02, and 1.8–18.2 in 2002–03).
[11] (abs) Lake trout restoration appears unlikely in northern Lake Michigan at current adult densities, and failure of restoration in Lake Champlain suggests that there are sources of high mortality that occur after fry emergence.
[12] (abs) INDEX WORDS: Lake trout, restoration, habitat, spawning, fry emergence.
[13] (res) In Parry Sound and Lake Michigan, all sites surveyed had rounded substrates, except for Bar Island where substrates were more angular.
[14] (res) While there was a wide range of particle sizes, particularly in Lake Champlain, substrates were mostly rubble and small cobbles.
[15] (res) In Lake Michigan substrate was primarily limestone, whereas in Parry Sound it was granite.
[16] (res) In Lake Champlain the surficial geology is more diverse and is comprised of marble, conglomerate, quartzite, granite, and dolomite.
[17] (res) Natural sites were characterized by rounded and angular cobble/rubble substrate, or flat bedrock.
[18] (res) Silt and organic material were absent or present in small quantities; over all sites, Lake Michigan had more zebra mussels, periphyton, and siltation than the other two lakes.
[19] (res) In Lake Champlain, fine silts were not present in shallow water (< 22 m) except at Allen Hill (0.3–0.8 m), which had the shortest fetch and was thickly coated with fines.
[20] (res) At sites where surveys extended below 22 m (Willsboro Bay, Ore Den Bay, Iron Bay) we found thick (> 2 cm) deposits of silt that filled interstitial spaces.
[21] (res) Ten of the fifteen sites in Lake Champlain and one site surveyed in Lake Michigan were manmade (breakwalls, mine tailings, water intake lines covered with rip-rap, and a ruined pier), with angular rubble-cobble substrates.
[22] (res) Man-made sites were in shallow water (< 7 m).
[23] (res) Of the sites where fall aggregations of lake trout had been reported, only two were classified as poor spawning sites (Shelburne Point and Thompson's Point); both were in Lake Champlain, and were primarily bedrock with no interstices.
[24] (res) Observations of adult lake trout aggregating at spawning sites provided an alternate method for assessing relative lake trout abundance (e.g., Marsden and Janssen 1997).
[25] (res) In Lakes Michigan, Huron, and Ontario, lake trout were observed in the range of 0.2 to 2 lake trout seen per minute during the day.
[26] (res) In our investigation, no lake trout were observed in Parry Sound, and low numbers were seen at two sites (LTB crib and Bay Harbor) in Lake Michigan.
[27] (res) A maximum of approximately 20 fish were seen in one 1-hr dive at the LTB crib, and five fish at Bay Harbor.
[28] (res) In Lake Champlain, lake trout were occasionally observed at Whallon Bay while diving, and at Arnold Bay from the surface (less than two per hour).
[29] (res) Lake trout were both seen and heard leaping at the surface during the evening at Whallon Bay, Grand Isle, and Arnold Bay.
[30] (res) At Grand Isle, large numbers of lake trout were regularly seen along the distal third of the breakwall in dense, horizontal columns of fish approximately 5–7 fish wide extending over 10 m.
[31] (res) Divers estimated that several hundred fish were present at the site; there were too many to count with confidence.
[32] (res) These fish were not sampled in our daytime gillnet sets, likely because the nets were highly visible in shallow water during the day.
[33] (res) Use of egg traps and nets in Lake Champlain provided data on when eggs were being deposited.
[34] (res) The last date on which egg traps and nets were retrieved with eggs in them was between late November and mid-December.
[35] (res) Egg bags were retrieved each year between mid-November and early December; thus, we may not have collected eggs deposited late in the spawning season.
[36] (res) This would reduce the total count of eggs, but likely does not affect the relative estimates of egg deposition among reefs.
[37] (res) Fry that had overwintered in egg bags were collected on both reefs sampled in Lake Champlain, two of three sampled in Parry Sound, and one of four sites sampled in Lake Michigan.
[38] (res) Fry collections in egg bags were highest at Grand Isle (mean 107 fry• m–2) in Lake Champlain, and similar among the LTB crib (12 ± 26 fry•m–2) in Lake Michigan and Davy (12 ± 27 fry• m–2) and Bar (12 ± 32 fry• m–2) Island sites in Parry Sound.
[39] (res) Fry aEgg bags were all deployed in late summer prior to the onset of spawning; only retrieval dates are given.
[40] (res) Egg traps were usually deployed prior to egg deposition; only the range of dates when eggs were collected are listed. bEggs from traps were not tallied separately on this date, so the SE could not be calculated. emergence as measured by fry traps yielded similar results – high fry density and CPUE in Lake Champlain (0 to 907.5 fry• m–2 and 0 to 3.6 fry• trap–1• day–1), lower densities in Parry Sound (0 to 9• m–2 and 0 to 0.06 fry• trap–1• day–1), and no emergent fry captured in Lake Michigan.
[41] (res) The number of fry emerging per 100 eggs estimated from fry traps was 0.12 to 6.8 in Parry Sound in 2002 and 2003, and 11.7 to 14.5 in Lake Champlain in 2003.
[42] (res) Estimates of fry hatch (fry per 100 eggs) measured with egg bag collections and emergence measured with fry traps followed similar patterns at most sites: 6.8 and 8.9, respectively, at Davy Is. and 0.8 and 2.3 at Bar Is. in Parry Sound in 2001–02, 14.5 and 18.2 at Grand Is. in Lake Champlain in 2002–03.
[43] (res) The number of hatched fry in egg bags compared with egg density estimated in bags removed in fall was lowest in Lake Champlain (0.4–1.1%), and similar in Lake Michigan (7.6%) and Parry Sound (2.3–8.9%) in 2001–02.
[44] (res) TABLE 3.
[45] (res) Summary of lake trout egg deposition in Lake Champlain, Parry Sound, and Lake Michigan, 2000–02.
[46] (res) Eggs were collected in egg traps or in egg bags buried in the substrate.
[47] (res) Collections in egg traps are reported as mean number of eggs•trap-1•day-1; collections from egg bags are reported as mean number of eggs•m-2 ± SD.
[48] (dis) Overall, we found that the proportion of reefs visited by lake trout, number of adult lake trout, density of eggs deposited, and number of fry hatched were highest in Lake Champlain, intermediate in Lake Huron, and the lowest in Lake Michigan.
[49] (dis) The availability and quality of spawning sites appear to be similar in all three lakes, but measured egg densities vary substantially among lakes and among sites within lakes.
[50] (dis) While these results explain the absence of detectable recruitment in Lake Michigan, it is more difficult to explain why recruitment is low in Lake Champlain compared with Parry Sound.
[51] (dis) TABLE 4.
[52] (dis) Lake trout fry collections in fry traps in Lake Champlain and Parry Sound, 2001–03.
[53] (dis) Fry were collected in three designs of emergent fry traps: steel traps checked by divers (diver), and steel traps or soft traps checked by lifting to the surface (surface).
[54] (dis) Fry•m-2 was calculated as total number of fry divided by the total area under all the traps at a given site.
[55] (dis) Number of fry collected per trap-day was calculated only over the range of dates when fry were collected in traps.
[56] (dis) Number of fry•100 eggs-1 was calculated from quantitative estimates of eggs (from fall egg bags—Table 1) divided into quantitative estimates of fry (from diver traps) × 100.
[57] (dis) Surface fry traps did not yield quantitative estimates of fry per unit area.
[58] (dis) Na = data not available. for lake trout spawning appears to be highest in Lake Michigan, intermediate in Lake Champlain, and smallest in Parry Sound.
[59] (dis) In general, sites in Lake Michigan had higher levels of periphyton and higher water clarity than in Lake Champlain; water clarity in Parry Sound was greater and the substrate was cleaner than in the other two lakes.
[60] (dis) Generally, there were no obvious differences in substrate size, cleanliness, reef contour, or reef size between sites with evidence of spawning, and sites without.
[61] (dis) High zebra mussel densities and high turbidity can negatively affect egg incubation by reducing entrapment of eggs and increasing siltation; however, sites in Lake Champlain with dense zebra mussels and low water clarity produced some of the highest fry hatch per egg seen in this study.
[62] (dis) More artificial sites than natural sites (6 versus 3) were used by spawning lake trout in Lake Champlain, and the only artificial site investigated in Lake Michigan produced the highest egg densities (LTB crib).
[63] (dis) No artificial sites were sampled in Parry Sound.
[64] (dis) The highest densities of eggs and fry were recovered from the smallest sites in lakes Champlain and Michigan.
[65] (dis) Sites in Parry Sound were of similar size and small relative to other lakes.
[66] (dis) It is possible that smaller sites concentrated spawning activity and eggs.

[67] (dis) Catches of adult lake trout in gillnets, while small, confirmed the patterns observed for egg deposition; the highest numbers were captured in Lake Champlain and no lake trout were captured in Lake Michigan surveys.
[68] (dis) There was a higher likelihood of seeing lake trout at smaller sites (Grand Isle, Arnold Bay, LTB crib), an indication of concentration around limited habitat.
[69] (dis) The absence of lake trout observed in Parry Sound is particularly puzzling, as the sites were very limited in area, and divers traversed the entire area of available spawning substrate during a related project during the spawning season.
[70] (dis) The extreme spawning density noted at the Grand Isle site in Lake Champlain likely results from attraction to effluent from a salmonid hatchery which enters the lake approximately 200 m from the breakwall.
[71] (dis) The highest egg density in a single egg bag was 31,577•m–2; in 2001 we observed windrows of an estimated several million eggs along the base of the breakwall at 7 m deep.
[72] (dis) These eggs were probably deposited on the breakwall and drifted to the base.
[73] (dis) While the high densities of zebra mussels on the breakwall may have inhibited entrainment of eggs into interstices, the extraordinary number of loose eggs may also indicate saturation of the interstitial spaces on the reef.
[74] (dis) Two weeks after the windrows were observed all eggs at the base of the breakwall were gone, presumably moved by currents and/or eaten by predators.
[75] (dis) Large schools of yellow perch (Perca flavescens) foraging intensively on the breakwall substrate, were videotaped at this site in late November, 2004; while we did not sample these fish, Fitzsimons (1990) documented yellow perch eating large quantities of lake trout eggs in Keuka Lake.
[76] (dis) There was substantial variation in egg densities within lakes and among years.
[77] (dis) Bags were buried in nearly identical locations in Parry Sound during 2001 and 2002 and substrate within all of the sites at Parry Sound was very homogeneous.
[78] (dis) Despite consistencies in sampling methodology, egg collections increased nearly 5-fold at Davy Is. (from a mean of 186 to 1,027 eggs•m–2) from 2001 to 2002, and decreased at Horse Is. and Mowat Is.
[79] (dis) Similarly, at Grand Isle in Lake Champlain egg collections decreased from a mean of 9,623 eggs•m–2 in 2001 to 3,183 eggs•m–2 in 2002.
[80] (dis) This within- and betweenyear variation in reproductive output may not affect long-term sustainability of lake trout populations in lakes where the mean egg density is high, but should be considered in annual estimates of recruitment potential Egg density and egg survival from Lake Champlain and Parry Sound were comparable to or greater than those measured in the other Great Lakes, whereas egg densities in Lake Michigan were substantially lower.
[81] (dis) Mean egg density in egg bags or similar samplers has been measured at 122–518 eggs•m–2 in Lake Superior, 6–6,178 eggs•m–2 in Lake Ontario, and 80–12,605•m–2 in southern Lake Michigan; the range we measured was 118–9,623 eggs•m–2 (median = 652) in Lake Champlain, 39–1,027 eggs•m–2 (median = 278) in Parry Sound, and 0.4–154.5•m–2 (median = 1.7) in northern Lake Michigan.
[82] (dis) These data suggest that egg density alone is not a good predictor of recruitment; for example, egg density in Parry Sound was lower than in southern Lake Michigan, where no recruitment has been seen.
[83] (dis) Fry hatch and emergence, measured with egg bags and fry traps respectively, were highest in Lake Champlain, intermediate in Parry Sound, and lowest in Lake Michigan.
[84] (dis) Numbers of fry collected in egg bags left in the substrate over winter reflect loss of eggs due to fungus and other sources of mortality.
[85] (dis) Fry traps provide relative measures of abundance between hatching and emergence.
[86] (dis) If we assume that fry catches in traps which remain in place throughout the emergence period, represent only the number of fry emerging from a limited area under and adjacent to each trap, it is possible to compare with fall egg densities and estimate a relative proportion of eggs that hatched.
[87] (dis) This comparison indicates that substantially more fry emerged per 100 eggs in Lake Champlain than Parry Sound.
[88] (dis) However, fry move laterally within the substrate prior to emergence (Marsden, unpublished data), variations in habitat structure may bias this assumption.
[89] (dis) To account for variation, we also determined fry hatch from egg bags that were covered and left in the substrate overwinter.
[90] (dis) These data suggest a low fry hatch in Lake Champlain relative to the other two lakes.
[91] (dis) Hatch rates were likely underestimated at Grand Isle, Lake Champlain, in 2001–02 as large numbers of eggs deposited in the bags formed masses of fungus resulting in near complete mortality.
[92] (dis) In 2002–03, egg deposition was lower at Grand Isle, and an estimated 18.2% of the eggs hatched.
[93] (dis) Similarly, fry traps at Whallon Bay collected a considerably higher numbers of fry (11.7 fry per 100 eggs) relative to egg bags (1.8 fry per 100 eggs); this difference may be attributable movement through the substrate or high mortality of eggs in the egg bags.
[94] (dis) At Arnold Bay, Lake Champlain, swarms of sac fry were observed by divers when the substrate was disturbed; given that lake trout fry are rarely ever seen by divers (Marsden and Fitzsimons, pers. obs.), this observation suggests that fry hatch was extremely high at this site.
[95] (dis) Estimates of egg survival in Lake Champlain were similar to measurements in Lake Ontario, which ranged from 12.4–16.5%.
[96] (dis) Densities of fry measured with emergent fry traps in Lake Ontario (2–289 fry•m–2) and Lake Superior (20–46 fry•m–2) were generally higher than those we measured in Parry Sound (0.6–9.3 fry•m–2) but similar to or lower than densities in Lake Champlain (1.5–907.5 fry•m–2; Fitzsimons et al. 2004).
[97] (dis) If we use Parry Sound as a benchmark for successful restoration of trout, the low use of spawning reefs in northern Lake Michigan indicates that the density of spawning lake trout is too low to support natural recruitment (Bronte et al. 2003a, 2003b).
[98] (dis) Lake trout assessments suggest that adult stocks are too low in northern Lake Michigan for restoration to occur (Bronte et al. 2003a).
[99] (dis) Selgeby et al. (1995) conducted a comprehensive synthesis of gillnet catch-rates to define a relative index of spawning lake trout necessary to produce measurable recruitment (17 to 135 lake trout•305 m–1 of gillnet).
[100] (dis) Adult abundance levels measured at historically important offshore spawning locations in northern Lake Michigan in 1999–2001 ranged from 0 to 145, but most sites were well below acceptable levels for recruitment and the majority of sites were not even visited by spawning lake trout (Bronte et al. 2003a).
[101] (dis) Low stocking rates, high mortality, or combinations of both likely contribute to the low abundance of adult lake trout in northern Lake Michigan.
[102] (dis) Exploitation by sport and tribal fisheries had been high, and in recent years mortality due to sea lamprey has increased substantially.
[103] (dis) In contrast to Lake Michigan, spawning reef use, abundance of adults, egg density, and fry hatch are high enough, in Lake Champlain than would be needed to support recruitment.
[104] (dis) Data on adult abundance to compare with the Great Lakes fall gillnetting data are not available, as fall assessments use electroshocking and gillnet surveys were only conducted in summer.
[105] (dis) The proportion of unclipped lake trout in the adult population in Lake Champlain is low (< 4%), with the apparent exception of one year class.
[106] (dis) Previous work on lake trout restoration has focused on bottlenecks to survival during the stages between egg deposition and emergence.
[107] (dis) Data from Lake Champlain suggest that high mortality is likely occurring after fry emerge.
[108] (dis) Further research in Lake Champlain and other lakes that also lack exotic species as a source of post-emergent mortality may further our understanding of mechanisms driving lake trout recruitment failures in the Great Lakes.
[109] (dis) The abundance of adult lake trout necessary for restoration may be related to the amount and size of spawning habitat available.
[110] (dis) At one extreme, high densities of eggs over limited habitat may be detrimental to egg survival, due to transmission of fungus among densely packed eggs, and saturation of interstices.
[111] (dis) In contrast, in northern Lake Michigan, a similar abundance of spawners over the many large spawning reefs may produce egg densities that could sustain reproduction (Jonas et al. in press).
[112] (dis) To achieve measurable fry production, stocking efforts need to focus on achieving optimal spawner densities per unit area of habitat.
[113] (dis) Research efforts should focus on investigating factors, that affect site fidelity and attraction to spawning reefs.
[114] (dis) In large lakes, target spawner abundance levels should be tailored to match regional and reef specific characteristics rather than striving to rebuild lake-wide populations.
